cbv22:0.2: The Discourse that Set the Dhamma Wheel Rolling
cbv22:1.1: Reverence to him, the Fortunate One, the Worthy One, the Perfect Sambuddha
cbv22:10.1: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of suffering” refers (i.e. suffering itself) ought to be fully known -
cbv22:10.2: to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things
cbv22:10.3: vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose,
cbv22:12.1: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the arising of suffering” refers (i.e. craving) ought to be given up -
cbv22:12.2: to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things
cbv22:12.3: vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose,
cbv22:14.1: Now that to which this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering” refers (i.e. Nibbāna) ought to be experienced -
cbv22:14.2: to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things
cbv22:14.3: vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose,
cbv22:16.1: Now that to which “this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the end of suffering” refers (i.e. the practice itself) -
cbv22:16.3: to me, monks, regarding these previously unheard-of things
cbv22:16.4: vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom rose,
cbv22:22.1: The Gods of the Sense World
cbv22:25.1: Having heard the cry of the gods called the Four Great Kings
cbv22:25.2: the Tāvatiṁsa gods let loose a cry:
cbv22:26.1: “The Fortunate One, while near Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana,
cbv22:26.2: has set rolling the unsurpassed Dhamma Wheel,
cbv22:26.3: and it cannot be rolled back by an ascetic or by a brahmin
cbv22:26.4: or by a god or by a demon or by a deity or by anyone in the world.”
